title: Teach the model your writing voice
description: From three samples of your own writing to a style sheet the model follows, checked on a real draft.
brief: The reader pastes three pieces they wrote themselves (emails, posts, a page). The model studies them and writes a short style sheet: typical sentence length, how they open and close, words and phrases they use, words they never use, how formal they are, how they use humour, punctuation habits. Then it rewrites a draft the reader supplies in that voice, and lists the three places it had to guess. The point is to stop AI text sounding like AI text by sounding like the reader instead.

title: Turn a rough ask into a prompt that works
description: Hand it a vague request and get back a tight prompt, tested on a sample before you use it.
brief: The reader types what they want in a sentence or two, badly. The model asks the questions that would change the result most (audience, length, format, what good looks like, what to avoid), then writes a reusable prompt with the answers built in, runs it once on a small sample so the reader can see the output, and tightens it based on what was weak. The reader ends with a prompt they can paste every time, not a one-off answer.

title: Check the facts in a piece before it goes out
description: Every claim in your draft listed, rated for how sure the model is, and marked for what to verify where.
brief: The reader pastes a draft (article, post, sales page, email). The model pulls out every factual claim as a numbered list, rates each one well documented, plausible but unverified, or from memory and worth checking, says what source would settle it, and flags numbers, dates, names and quotes especially. It does not invent sources. It then returns the draft with the risky claims marked so the reader can check them before publishing. Honest about the fact the model cannot browse.

title: Build a slide deck from a topic
description: A deck planned slide by slide: one point per slide, the words on it, the speaker notes, and what to leave out.
brief: The reader gives the topic, the audience, how long they have to speak and what they want the room to do afterwards. The model asks a few questions, then plans the deck: a slide count that fits the time, and for each slide a title, the one point, the words that go on the slide (few), the speaker notes in full sentences, and any chart or image needed. It ends with the three slides it would cut if the talk ran long. Output in a form that can be pasted into PowerPoint, Google Slides or Canva.

title: Turn one recording into five pieces of content
description: A podcast or video transcript becomes a newsletter, a LinkedIn post, three short posts and a set of quotes, in your voice.
brief: The reader pastes a transcript of a podcast episode, webinar or video they made. The model first lists the five strongest ideas in it with timestamps if present, then writes: a newsletter section, one LinkedIn post, three short posts for Instagram or X, and five quotable lines taken word for word from the transcript. Everything stays true to what was said, no new claims. The reader chooses which ideas to use before the writing starts.

title: Set up a weekly competitor check
description: A recurring brief for Claude routines or ChatGPT tasks that watches three competitors and reports in five lines.
brief: The reader names up to three competitors and what they care about (prices, new offers, hiring, content themes). The model writes the instructions for a scheduled task that runs weekly: which pages to look at, what counts as a change worth reporting, how to write the five-line report, and what to ignore. It also writes the first report format as an example. Includes a note on setting it up as a Claude routine or a ChatGPT scheduled task, and that a check only reports what it could read.

title: Turn a talk or video into a LinkedIn post
description: From a transcript to one post with a hook, one story and one lesson, under 200 words.
brief: The reader pastes a transcript or their notes from a talk, video or client call. The model picks the single most useful moment, writes a LinkedIn post built on it: a first line that earns the click on 'see more', one story told plainly, one lesson, and a last line that invites a reply rather than selling. Under 200 words, no hashtags walls, no emojis unless the reader uses them. Offers two alternative first lines.

title: Write to ten ideal customers, one by one
description: A list definition, then a personal first email for each person built from what they've put in public, without pretending to look anything up.
brief: The reader describes who they sell to and what they sell. The model helps define the list (role, company size, signals that someone needs this now), then for each of ten people the reader pastes a few lines about (their LinkedIn headline, a recent post, their website line) it writes a short first email: one thing noticed about them, one line on the problem, one easy ask. Under 90 words each. The model does not claim to find email addresses or browse profiles; the reader brings the details.

title: Mine your best posts for the next ten
description: Paste your twenty best-performing posts and get the pattern behind them, then ten new posts that use it.
brief: The reader pastes their best posts from any platform, with the numbers if they have them. The model works out what they have in common: topics, openings, length, structure, the feeling they create. It writes that up as five rules, then drafts ten new posts that follow the rules on topics the reader hasn't covered yet. It says which of the ten is the safest bet and which is the experiment.

title: Rewrite a page in plain English
description: Your page or email made readable by a tired person on a phone, with the meaning kept and the jargon gone.
brief: The reader pastes a page, email or document that is too long or too clever. The model rewrites it so a reader with no background understands it on the first read: short sentences, everyday words, one idea per paragraph, the most important thing first. It keeps every fact and promise, and shows a short list of what it cut and why. Optional: a version at half the length.

title: Subject lines and preview text for any email
description: Three subject lines and a preview line for the email you paste, each with the reason it should work, none that overpromise.
brief: The reader pastes an email they've written. The model proposes three subject lines in different styles (plain, curious, specific), a preview line that adds to the subject rather than repeating it, and a sentence on why each might get opened by this list. Under 50 characters where possible, no clickbait, no exclamation marks, nothing the email doesn't deliver. The reader can ask for versions for a cold list or a warm list.

title: A month of posts from one idea bank
description: Thirty posts planned from the ten things you know best, with a picture direction for each, batched by week.
brief: The reader lists the ten things they could talk about for an hour, their platform, and how often they can post. The model turns them into a 30-post plan: for each post a hook line, the point, the format (text, carousel, short video, photo) and a one-line image direction a designer or Canva could follow. Grouped into four weeks with a theme each, so content can be made in one sitting a week. No hashtags lists, no filler posts like 'motivation Monday'.

title: Twenty short video scripts from customer questions
description: Every question customers ask becomes a script under 30 seconds with its on-screen text line, ready for bulk production.
brief: The reader pastes the questions customers ask them (from emails, DMs, calls). The model writes a script for each: a first line that states the question, a plain answer in two or three sentences, and the one line of text to show on screen. Each under 30 seconds spoken. Formatted as a table or CSV so it can go straight into Canva's bulk create or a teleprompter. It groups the questions by theme and flags any that need a longer video instead.

title: Study an account that's winning in your space
description: Paste ten of their captions and learn what they do, what to borrow, what to leave alone, then three posts of yours in that structure.
brief: The reader pastes ten captions or post texts from an account doing well in their niche, with rough engagement if known. The model identifies the structures (how they open, how long, what they ask, how they use proof), separates what's worth borrowing from what's their personality, and writes three posts for the reader in the borrowed structures on the reader's own topics. It never copies lines and says so. Honest that it cannot see images, video or the account itself.

title: LinkedIn posts that bring the right DMs
description: Five posts that make the right person message you first, with a soft ask and a reply you've prepared.
brief: The reader says who they want to hear from and what they sell. The model writes five LinkedIn posts designed to get a message rather than a like: a specific problem the right person recognises, a sign of how the reader solves it, and an invitation to reply or DM that doesn't feel like a pitch. For each post, the model also writes the first reply the reader sends when someone messages. No 'DM me the word GROWTH' tactics.

title: Turn one long piece into a week of short posts
description: An article, newsletter or long post broken into seven short posts that each stand alone.
brief: The reader pastes one long piece. The model finds seven ideas in it that work on their own, writes a short post for each (one for each day), in the reader's voice, each with a different opening type: a question, a number, a mistake, a story, a contrast, a how-to, a one-liner. Nothing is repeated across the seven. It suggests the order to post them and which one to pin.

title: News snippets with your take, from today's links
description: Paste three headlines or links and get three short posts that say what happened and what it means for your audience, with nothing invented.
brief: The reader pastes today's headlines, article text or links, because the model has no live news and must not invent any. For each, the model writes a three-line snippet: what happened in one plain sentence, why it matters to the reader's audience, and one practical thing to do or watch. It marks any claim it can't confirm from the text given. Optional: the same three as a short newsletter section.

title: Read your TikTok or Instagram export
description: Upload or paste your account's data export and get what worked, what didn't, and three experiments for next month.
brief: The reader uploads or pastes the analytics export from TikTok or Instagram (posts with views, likes, saves, shares, follows). The model finds the ten best and ten worst posts, works out what the best share (topic, length, format, hook, posting time), checks the pattern against the worst ones, and proposes three experiments for next month with the number that would show each one worked. It states what the export doesn't tell it and doesn't guess at the algorithm.

title: Reply to a batch of comments and DMs in your voice
description: Paste twenty comments or messages and get a reply for each that sounds like you, sorted by what needs a human.
brief: The reader pastes a batch of comments and DMs and a few examples of how they usually reply. The model sorts them: thanks, questions, complaints, spam, and leads. It writes a short reply for each in the reader's voice, flags the ones a human should answer personally (complaints, leads, anything about money), and leaves spam unanswered. Replies stay short and specific to what the person said.

title: Write your bio and your pinned post
description: A profile line that says who it's for and what you do, and a pinned post that tells a new visitor what to do next.
brief: The reader says what they do, who it's for, and what they want a new visitor to do (follow, DM, click). The model writes a bio in the platform's length limit (it asks which platform), three options from plain to bold, and a pinned post that introduces the reader in a few lines, shows one proof point and gives the next step. No buzzwords like 'helping you unlock your potential'.

title: Turn a book's ideas into original posts
description: From your notes on a book, not its text: ten posts that apply its ideas to your audience, credited properly.
brief: The reader pastes their own notes or highlights from a book they've read and says who their audience is. The model writes ten posts or short articles that apply the book's ideas to that audience's situation, with original examples, crediting the book and author in one line each. It does not reproduce the book's text, and it says when a note is too thin to build on. The result is content that reads as the reader's thinking, informed by the book.

title: Turn a video into a blog post that ranks
description: A transcript becomes an article with headings, a summary, and the questions people search, not a transcript with paragraph breaks.
brief: The reader pastes a video transcript and the one search phrase they want the post to answer. The model restructures the content as an article: a title with the phrase, a two-sentence summary, headings that match how people search, the body rewritten as prose, a short FAQ of three questions the video answered, and a place to embed the video. It cuts spoken filler and repeats. Under 1,500 words unless the reader asks.

title: Write an article with internal links placed where they help
description: Paste your list of pages and the article links to them naturally, with the anchor text and the reason for each link.
brief: The reader gives the topic and search phrase, and pastes a list of their existing pages (URL and one-line description each). The model writes the article, and as it goes links to the reader's pages where a reader would actually want to go next, with natural anchor text. It ends with a table of every link placed, the anchor text, and why it's there, and names two pages the reader doesn't have but should. No link stuffing.

title: Answer the questions people ask about your topic
description: An FAQ page built from the questions customers actually ask, each answered in a way that could appear in search.
brief: The reader pastes the questions they hear from customers and a few from search suggestions. The model groups them, removes duplicates, writes a short direct answer to each (two to four sentences, the answer in the first line), suggests the order for the page, and marks which answers would benefit from a number, a screenshot or an example. It writes the page intro and says which three questions deserve their own article.

title: Read your ads export and decide what to cut, keep and test
description: Paste or upload a Meta or Google ads export and get the three decisions it supports, with the numbers behind each.
brief: The reader uploads or pastes the export from Meta Ads or Google Ads (campaigns and ads with spend, impressions, clicks, results, cost per result). The model finds what to switch off, what to leave alone, what to put more budget behind, and one test to run next, each with the figures that support it and the figure that would change the decision. It says what the export can't show (profit, lifetime value) and doesn't invent benchmarks.

title: A LinkedIn or Instagram carousel from one idea
description: Eight slides, one line each, with the image direction, built so the first slide earns the swipe.
brief: The reader gives one idea, lesson or process. The model writes an eight-slide carousel: slide one a hook that promises something specific, slides two to seven one point each in one or two lines, slide eight the takeaway and a soft call to action. For each slide a one-line note on the visual. It also writes the caption. Text short enough to read on a phone.

title: Build the prompt template you'll reuse every time
description: Your own one-page frame for briefing any model: who it's for, what you bring, what good looks like, what to avoid.
brief: The model helps the reader build a reusable prompt frame for their business: a short description of the business and audience to paste every time, the tone rules, the words to avoid, the format they usually want, and the questions the model should ask before starting. It builds the frame by asking the reader, then writes it as a block the reader saves and pastes at the top of any new conversation, with an example of it in use.

title: Spreadsheet formulas from plain English
description: Describe what the sheet has and what you want it to work out, and get the formula, what it does, and a way to check it.
brief: The reader describes their columns (with examples of the values) and the result they want in plain words. The model asks whether it's Excel or Google Sheets, writes the formula, explains each part in a sentence, gives a two-row example to test it on, and names the common mistake that would break it (text that looks like a number, blanks, dates). If a formula is the wrong tool and a pivot table or filter would be simpler, it says so.

title: Structured prompts for image and video generators
description: A fill-in frame for Midjourney, Flux, Veo or Runway prompts: subject, setting, light, lens, motion, with three variations.
brief: The reader describes the picture or clip they want in a sentence. The model turns it into a structured prompt with labelled parts: subject, action, setting, time and light, camera and lens, style references in general terms, aspect ratio, and for video the motion and duration. It gives the same prompt as a one-line version for tools that want prose and as a JSON block for tools that take structure, then three variations that change one thing each. It says which parts generators most often ignore.
